title: Dual UK-Iranian national arrested over RAF Fairford incident
description: A UK-Iranian dual national has been arrested on suspicion of preparation of terrorist acts in connection with the incident at RAF Fairford, counter-te
body: A UK-Iranian dual national has been arrested on suspicion of preparation of terrorist acts in connection with the incident at RAF Fairford, counter-terror police have said.The 25-year-old man was arrested in Westminster, London. Two properties in the area have been searched.Five men in their twenties who were arrested near the Gloucestershire airbase on Sunday remain on police bail. All five were UK nationals from London.Counter-terror police are considering "all possible angles - including foreign state involvement", the force's senior national coordinator Vicki Evans said."The investigation into circumstances surrounding events in Gloucestershire is hugely complex, and our specialist teams are interrogating multiple lines of enquiry," she said."I'd like to thank the public for their continued support and patience whilst we work through this investigation."Police had initially given the dual UK-Iranian national's age as 27 and said a second man had been questioned under caution, but in a later update said that this was not the case.Prime Minister Andy Burnham said on Wednesday there were "strong indications" that Iran played a part in the incident. He did not provide further details, and Tehran has strongly denied any involvement.The five men were arrested in the early hours of Sunday morning after "three suspicious vehicles" were reported travelling towards the base operated by the US Air Force (USAF), sparking a major security incident.The BBC understands that one of the men had dialled 999 himself, about an hour before a local farmer alerted police to a "large group" of masked men near the vehicles.They were arrested on suspicion of explosives offences and later on suspicion of preparing a terrorist act, before being released on bail on Monday in what police called an "investigative decision" that was "grounded in experience and strategy".Police said a quantity of petrol but no explosive devices were found during searches of vans near the site.The group were aged between 23 and 25. Four live in Westminster and one in Camden, and searches of their homes were carried out.US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Monday that "the hands of a foreign actor" had clearly been involved in the incident at the base, which has been used as a forward operating location by the USAF for decades.In recent months, US bombers have taken off from the airbase for the Middle East, after the UK approved a US request to use it for what it called defensive strikes on Iran.On Thursday, the British ambassador to Iran met the country's foreign ministry at the request of the Iranian government.

schema.headline: Dual UK-Iranian national arrested over RAF Fairford incident

title: What are the new rules in Scotland's supermarkets?
description: No more cereal at the end of the aisle? New rules in Scotland's supermarketsImage source, Getty ImagesUpdated 4 hours agoSugary soft drinks, biscuits
body: No more cereal at the end of the aisle? New rules in Scotland's supermarketsImage source, Getty ImagesUpdated 4 hours agoSugary soft drinks, biscuits and some breakfast cereals have disappeared from prominent positions in Scotland's supermarkets.The Scottish government has introduced rules meaning some products that are high in fat, sugar and salt can no longer be put in prime end-of-aisle slots, or feature as part of multi-buy offers in store or online.The regulations will apply to the usual suspects - chocolate, crisps, biscuits and ice cream.But it could also include kombucha, seaweed snacks, muesli and chewing gum, depending on their sugar content.The Scottish government regulations, external apply to businesses with more than 50 employees. This could include supermarkets, high street shops, restaurants, pharmacies, petrol stations and garden centres.They are are no longer allowed to display pre-packaged foods including sugary soft drinks, confectionery, biscuits and breakfast cereals in prominent locations such as entrances, checkouts, aisle ends and designated queueing areas. Image source, Scottish governmentPrice promotions on those items - such as "three for the price of two", "three for £10" or "buy five and save 20%" - are no longer allowed. Multi-buy offers, including extra loyalty points, are also banned. Another type of deal that falls foul of the rules is those offering a free high-sugar, fat or salt product alongside another purchase - for example, a free chocolate bar with a newspaper.There are no restrictions on discounts such as half-price or "save £1". Online retailers also face restrictions - including a ban on advertising some foods on their homepage.Similar restrictions are already in place in England and Wales. Chocolate, ice cream... what else? The short answer is: a lot, if there’s enough sugar, salt or fat packed into it. The restrictions could apply to: Drinks with added sugar - such as lemonade, soda, squash, chocolate milk, almond milk, ready-made coffee, kombucha, energy drinks, and hot chocolateSavoury snacks such as crisps and tortilla chips, and even lentil-based crisps and seaweed snacks, depending on their contentBreakfast cereals, granola, muesli and oat-based cereals Pre-made pizzas, roast potatoes, chips, fish fingers and chicken nuggetsReady meals, as well as pasta, rice or noodles with added ingredients or fillings, such as ravioli and tortelliniConfectionery, such as popcorn, chocolate, chewing gum and sweetsIce cream, sorbets, ice lollies, sponge cakes, custard, jelly, crumbles Cereal bars, biscuits, scones, flapjacks, doughnuts and Danish pastries Sweetened Greek-style, probiotic, kids' and drinking yoghurts Is this the end of the meal deal? Meal deals are exempt from the regulations, as are "dine for two" offers. However, any foods identified in the rules, whether part of a meal deal or not, cannot be placed in the restricted locations, such as supermarket entrances. The fight against obesityThe Scottish government regulations are being introduced to encourage healthier eating choices. Public Health Minister Maree Todd noted that two out of three Scottish adults are overweight or obese, with those living in the poorest areas worst affected. She said: "We know that promotions and prominent product placement can encourage over-consumption and impulse buying of foods with high levels of calories, fat, sugar and salt."By restricting the promotion of less healthy food and drink we can make it easier for people to make healthier choices, improving health and wellbeing, and create a Scotland where everyone eats well and has a healthy weight."

schema.headline: What are the new rules in Scotland's supermarkets?

title: NY governor appoints special counsel in Cornell frat rape investigation
description: Figure caption, Cornell students voice frustration at public hearing over rape caseBySareen HabeshianUpdated 7 hours agoNew York Governor Kathy Hochul
body: Figure caption, Cornell students voice frustration at public hearing over rape caseBySareen HabeshianUpdated 7 hours agoNew York Governor Kathy Hochul has appointed the state's attorney general, Letitia James, as a special prosecutor to investigate the alleged gang rape of a woman at Cornell University.The woman has alleged she was drugged and raped by several men at a fraternity house in 2024. The case was reopened after the woman filed a civil lawsuit last month that thrust the allegations into the national spotlight."New information has raised serious questions about how this case was handled, and I've lost faith in the Tompkins County DA's ability to fairly oversee it," Hochul said.The announcement means District Attorney Matthew Van Houten is no longer overseeing the case.The BBC has contacted Van Houten's office for comment. He has defended his office's previous decision not to file charges in the case, arguing they were not given enough evidence to meet the legal threshold. Van Houten reopened the case after the civil lawsuit and said much of the information released in recent weeks about the case was not passed to his office. "The young woman at the centre of this case deserves to know that every fact will be examined and justice pursued," Hochul said in a statement. James could prosecute any offences that might be found during her investigation and present evidence to a grand jury, Hochul said.James, who is the state's chief legal officer, said on X, external that she stood ready "to lead a process guided by the facts and the law"."The Governor has entrusted my office with this investigation, and we do not take that responsibility lightly," James added.Hochul and James are scheduled to provide an update on the investigation on Friday morning local time.Image source, Getty ImagesThe woman at the centre of the case, identified anonymously as Jane Doe in court documents, filed a civil lawsuit against the Ivy League university in September.Jane Doe is a placeholder name sometimes used in US law for privacy or anonymity reasons.She alleged that she was drugged and raped by seven men at a fraternity house at the university in 2024.She claimed that Cornell failed to protect her or adequately punish the men, who have now become known as the Cornell Seven. The case was initially referred to Van Houten, the top prosecutor in the county, in 2024.Van Houten said his office did not bring charges at the time because he had only seen a statement from Doe implying the incident was consensual and that she had not been drugged.This week, his office announced it would be reopening the case - less than two weeks after Doe filed her civil lawsuit.Cornell has said it provided evidence to the district attorney's office from its own investigation, including a Snapchat group chat in which fraternity members discussed a "free" sexual encounter with Doe on the night of the alleged assault.Doe's lawyer, Thomas Giuffra, has accused the district attorney of repeatedly changing his story amid news coverage of the case.

schema.headline: NY governor appoints special counsel in Cornell frat rape investigation

title: Smit Machchhar: Pilot of Flydubai flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv describes cockpit attack by co-pilot
description: The Indian pilot of the Flydubai plane who was attacked by his co-pilot and opened the cockpit door to let others in has said he was determined not to
body: The Indian pilot of the Flydubai plane who was attacked by his co-pilot and opened the cockpit door to let others in has said he was determined not to let others die.Capt Smit Machchhar said he was on the floor and still being attacked when he realised the plane carrying more than 170 passengers was sinking and he had to do something. "I was lying on the floor injured but I told myself to go for one last push to open the door from inside," he said in a video call with Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi."Others came in and also played a role [in controlling the situation]. I was of course fighting for my own life but at the same time I knew I was not going to let others die," he added.Flydubai's flight FZ1073, which was bound for Tel Aviv from Dubai early on Wednesday morning, plunged more than 17,000ft (5,200m) two and a half hours into its journey.It first sent an emergency signal to air traffic controllers before switching to code squawk 7500, which indicates hijacking.Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu later told the media that one pilot had stabbed the other before "apparently trying to crash" the plane.After fellow passengers overpowered the attacker, two reserve pilots, who were onboard, safely landed the plane at Tabuk Airport in north-western Saudi Arabia at 06:58 local time.Machchhar, who has been hailed as a "true hero" by Netanyahu, was taken to hospital in Tabuk before being airlifted to Abu Dhabi, where he is reported to be in a stable condition.Netanyahu told Fox News the attacker was an Omani national and said investigations suggested he had undergone "Islamist radical indoctrination".He said that once the attacker had been subdued and tied up by passengers and crew, he was "calling out to the aircrew 'kill me, kill me', so it's clear he was suicidal - that's not a question".The United Arab Emirates has begun investigating "whether the incident was linked to any terrorist activity or purpose", according to the country's state news agency.

schema.headline: Smit Machchhar: Pilot of Flydubai flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv describes cockpit attack by co-pilot

title: Manchester City: FA says guilty verdict has "significant implications for integrity of the game"
description: City will claim as part of their appeal that key sponsorship deals were funded by the Abu Dhabi government, rather than the club's owners.Owners Abu D
body: City will claim as part of their appeal that key sponsorship deals were funded by the Abu Dhabi government, rather than the club's owners.Owners Abu Dhabi United Group (ADUG) - a private investment company belonging to United Arab Emirates vice-president and deputy prime minister Sheikh Mansour - are said to have topped up the value of commercial deals as part of a "disguised funding scheme" to the scale of £830.69m.This, it was argued, enabled the club to appear to comply with Premier League and Uefa financial rules.Premier League rules allow state-owned bodies to sponsor clubs.City's principal sponsor Etihad Airways has said it is considering legal action against the Premier League, claiming the release of the commission findings had "damaging implications… despite the airline not being named in the redacted published findings".The UAE's state-owned national airline said it "categorically rejects any finding, conclusion or implication that suggests the airline has ever been involved in improper commercial arrangements".Etihad is owned by sovereign wealth fund L'Imad which is chaired by the Crown Prince of Abu Dhabi, the son of the UAE president.

schema.headline: Manchester City: FA says guilty verdict has "significant implications for integrity of the game"

title: Olivia Dean accused of copying Bill Withers' Just The Two of Us
description: British pop star Olivia Dean has been accused of copying the melody of Bill Withers' soul classic Just The Two of Us in a legal case filed in Californ
body: British pop star Olivia Dean has been accused of copying the melody of Bill Withers' soul classic Just The Two of Us in a legal case filed in California.The complaint centres around Dean's song I've Seen It, taken from her Brit Award-winning 2025 album The Art of Loving.Just The Two of Us was a hit for Withers in 1981, and the publishers of the late singer's catalogue allege that the two songs "share musical features" that are "so striking" they cannot have arisen by coincidence alone.The lawsuit names Dean's record label Capitol Records, parent company Universal Music Group and her publishing companies as the defendants. It does not seek damages from the singer herself or her co-writers Bastian Langebæk and Max Wolfgang.In legal documents seen by the BBC, Mattie Music Group, which looks after Withers' back catalogue, said it hired a musicologist to review the two songs.He concluded "that the works contain substantial similarities" including the "repeated copying" of the melody from Just The Two of Us, the documents said.The publishers claim they notified Dean's record label of the potential infringement in August, but the music was not pulled from distribution.To prove plagiarism, Mattie Music Group would have to prove that Dean and her co-writers had previously heard Withers' original composition.In the lawsuit, they allege that his song's "extraordinary and sustained" commercial success, including "decades of radio play", would mean the musicians had "reasonable opportunity" to have encountered Just The Two of Us before writing I've Seen It.The defendants have yet to respond to the lawsuit. The BBC has contacted them, and Dean's representatives, for a comment.I've Seen It is the closing track of Dean's breakthrough album, which was released in September 2025.A sweet, acoustic ballad, it discusses the various types of love she's encountered in her life - from high school crushes to the love she has for her family and friends.Speaking to W Magazine last year, she said the song was written after "I'd had a lot of red wine". "When I heard it back for the first time, I burst into tears. It felt like the loveliest note to end on. Whether it's within your friends, your family, or just the love that exists in the strangers around you, it's there, and it's inside of you, too."It is has been streamed on Spotify about 246 million times, while Just The Two of Us has racked up 948 million plays.Withers' track went to number two in the US charts in 1981 and earned him a Grammy for best R&B song. He died in 2020.Dean picked up best new artist at this year's Grammys, while The Art of Loving reached number three in the US and number one in the UK, and was named album of the year at the Brit Awards.

schema.headline: Olivia Dean accused of copying Bill Withers' Just The Two of Us

title: Why Gen Z are opting out of workplace pensions
description: 'It could cost me £10k but I need the money now': Why Gen Z are opting out of pensionsImage source, Hassan NassarImage caption, Dr Hassan Nassar is de
body: 'It could cost me £10k but I need the money now': Why Gen Z are opting out of pensionsImage source, Hassan NassarImage caption, Dr Hassan Nassar is determined to opt back in to his pension as soon as he canUntil early September, Hassan Nassar, 26, was saving around £430 every month into his NHS workplace pension.But the trainee GP, who works in the West Midlands, says he was "really cash strapped" and decided to stop putting money aside for around "six to 12 months".He needs the money to help take care of a sick family member, save for his first home and cover rent and student loan repayments.But he's aware there is a cost to opting out, estimating he could lose between "£5,000 and £10,000" in future retirement income due to the decades of compound interest he will miss out on by not saving now."People will say, you're silly, look at what you'll be missing out in the future," he tells the BBC. "But I need to look at what I'd be losing now if I didn't opt out."Future problemsAll employees will be automatically enrolled, external in a workplace pension if they are aged 22 or above and earn over £10,000, although there are exceptions.A percentage is taken directly from the worker's pay - usually around 5% - with tax relief added on top, and the employer must also pay a minimum contribution on top. But a growing number of Gen Z and millennials are opting out of these schemes due to cost-of-living pressures and the government has warned they could be on track for lower private pension incomes than people retiring today.That is a problem, because while most people in the UK will eventually get a state pension, it only provides a minimum level of retirement income and many will rely on a private pension to supplement it.Image source, Guido Mieth via Getty ImagesHassan says he was paying 10.7% of his gross earnings each month into his workplace pension, while the NHS contributed a substantial amount on top.But unlike some employers, the NHS doesn't allow staff to reduce their contributions when times are hard.  Overall, however, he is confident he will have enough to retire on at the end of his "30-40" year career and is determined to opt back in to his pension as soon as he can. According to the Department for Work and Pensions (DWP), around 22.6 million people, or 90% of those who are eligible for "automatic enrolment" pensions, are paying into one, while about 2.5 million are not. However, Pensions Minister Torsten Bell told the BBC that "a rising number of young workers aren't saving, and overall there is a danger tomorrow's retirees are on track for lower private pension incomes than today's".'How can I save for a house?'Evie, 22, from Cornwall, says she opted out of entering the workplace pension at the London events company she works for.A recent drama school graduate, she says she would have struggled to cover her outgoings, including food, travel and the £800 she pays in rent. Evie is conscious about missing out on saving for retirement, but there are other things she needs money for that make it impractical right now. "How can I save for a house, how can I save for a car and afford my outgoings? I don't want to just work day in, day out to live, I want to work to have a life."'Think of your future self'April Leeson, from The Private Office, a chartered financial advice firm, says she would always advise people to not stop paying into their pensions if they can help it, even if that means reducing their contributions, which many employers allow you to do.This is partly because of the free employer contributions they will miss out on but also the lost compound interest."The current minimum pension age is 57, so any money you save in your 20s will have at least 30 years to compound and grow."£100 saved now, compounded at 4% a year over 30 years, is going to be worth a lot more than £100 saved in 15 to 20 years' time."She also urges younger people to think ahead. "You really need to think of your future self and what that person will need to retire comfortably."Kharlee, 47, a teacher from South East London, can certainly relate to this. She stopped her contributions to a workplace pension twice over the last five years for financial reasons. Image caption, Kharlee worries she won't have a comfortable retirementAnd she thinks she missed out on saving about £5,000 into her pension pot.She's in a better place financially now, but recently became self-employed and is no longer part of a private pension scheme, something she hopes to change."I would like to feel my pension is secure, and I don't feel like that. I worry I'm not going to be able to live comfortably at the age of retirement."Get in touchAre you able to save money every month? Share your tips with us on how you do it.

schema.headline: Why Gen Z are opting out of workplace pensions

title: What's really going on in lymphatic drainage beauty trend videos?
description: Image source, Abbey AlexandraImage caption, Abbey Alexandra performs lymphatic drainage massages a couple of times a weekByEmily HoltIf she's ever fee
body: Image source, Abbey AlexandraImage caption, Abbey Alexandra performs lymphatic drainage massages a couple of times a weekByEmily HoltIf she's ever feeling bloated, Abbey Alexandra has a go-to routine, using body oil and a wooden roller to perform stomach massages.She shares before-and-after videos on TikTok, saying she feels the process leaves her depuffed and defined: "You definitely feel a lot better after, they are relaxing."The technique is a form of lymphatic drainage massage, adapted from a medical treatment and shared as a beauty trend. Celebrity fans include Maya Jama, who shares her clinic sessions, and actress Hailey Bieber, who told Time magazine: "I swear by them."Whether there is a physical change - or any need for one - is debatable, but fans of the massages claim they help "flatten" and "debloat" and give a "snatched waist" and "sculpted abs". But what's actually happening to their bodies?What do the videos show?Image source, Abbey AlexandraImage caption, Before-and-after video grabs of a form of lymphatic drainage massage Many videos on social media promoting lymphatic massage show a woman either standing sideways, facing the front or perhaps lying down with her stomach showing a slight - and very normal - curve outwards.Then begins the methodical massage in circular motions seemingly draining fluid away. By the end, her stomach appears flatter - if a little red.But social media body trends should always be viewed with scepticism, says Dr Ella Guest, senior research fellow and health psychologist at the Centre for Appearance Research based at the University of the West of England."These images might be altered using photo-editing tools or filters, people standing in particular poses, use of lighting, lots could even be AI-generated," she says."I think stopping to reflect on what you see and questioning whether it looks realistic, or if it's very aligned with beauty standards, can be useful. Remember, if something looks too good to be true, it probably is."What is the lymphatic system? The lymphatic system is a network of channels and glands throughout the body that helps fight infection and remove excess fluid, according to the NHS.Dr Xand van Tulleken tells Morning Live that the lymphatic system helps remove excess fluid from tissues and supports the immune system."When it is not working properly, it can contribute to swelling, which can be a condition called lymphoedema."This commonly affects people who have cancers that involve the lymph system or who've had treatment involving the lymph nodes.It causes swelling in any part of the body, but usually develops in the arms or legs."In simple terms, the lymphatic system helps keep your body's fluid levels balanced, cleans up waste, and supports your defences against illness," says van Tulleken.Draining your lymphatic systemDr Xand explains how to drain your lymphatic system.What's the massage doing?Image source, Abbey AlexandraImage caption, Abbey says lymphatic drainage massage makes her feel less bloatedDr Xand says manual lymphatic drainage is one of a range of treatments used by medical professionals "if your lymphatic system isn't working as it should". He describes it as using "light pressure" and "strategic massage techniques" to "clear" your lymphatic system. "They'll coax excess lymph fluid from your swollen tissues toward your lymph nodes, where the lymph can reabsorb," he says - adding lymph nodes are found in the armpits, neck and groin. He adds that these massages can be a "safe way" to relieve symptoms for conditions like lymphoedema but are not suitable for some people with pre-existing medical conditions. He stresses: "No one should get their health advice from Instagram - far safer to use the NHS website, or consult your GP."Abbey, who has endometriosis which she says causes her to feel bloated, began doing her own massage routines twice a week aer seeing social media posts about lymphatic drainage."I started using my hands and then I bought some wooden tools as well."After doing my routine, I personally feel less puffy and bloated, particularly around my stomach."Visually, I notice that my stomach looks a little more defined and I also feel lighter and more comfortable."Does it work?Figure caption, Draining your lymphatic systemDr Xand says there is "no need" for most people to perform lymphatic drainage treatments at home."There is very little high-quality evidence showing they provide meaningful or lasting benefits for healthy individuals, and it does not promote fat loss," he says.But he does note that lymphatic drainage massages can feel "relaxing" and some people "can notice a temporary reduction in swelling"."For most healthy people, regular movement, exercise and staying hydrated are all that's needed to support normal lymphatic function," he says."Unless someone has a diagnosed lymphatic condition, I don't think anyone needs routine lymphatic drainage treatments, despite the growing popularity of these practices on social media."For Abbey, it's something she enjoys. "I know the visual difference is temporary... But I do like how I look and feel afterwards so it'll always be a part of my routine."However, Guest warns striving for a sculpted stomach could "feed into people's insecurities"."We know that when we compare ourselves online and try to live up to these trends, we tend to scrutinise our appearance more and feel less satisfied with how we look," she says."The reality is that healthy bodies come in a wide range of shapes and sizes."

schema.headline: What's really going on in lymphatic drainage beauty trend videos?

title: First minister demands 'new deal' for Wales, before Plaid Cymru conference
description: Ap Iorwerth hosted the pro-independence first ministers of Scotland and Northern Ireland in Cardiff last month and jointly declared that "Westminster'
body: Ap Iorwerth hosted the pro-independence first ministers of Scotland and Northern Ireland in Cardiff last month and jointly declared that "Westminster's time is coming to an end".In his 2,000-word letter to Burnham, ap Iorwerth made a detailed case for the transfer of powers over policing and justice, rail infrastructure and the Crown Estate, external to Wales.He also called for "funding arrangements that are fair, needs-based and reflect Wales' demographic and economic realities".He said that "Wales' constitutional settlement should continue to evolve to improve democratic accountability, boost growth, strengthen public services and deliver better outcomes for our communities".Speaking to BBC Radio Wales Breakfast, ap Iorwerth said he was looking for "practical answers to unlock those things that we need to take Wales forward".He said he recognised there could be "practical barriers" to how the Crown Estate was devolved, and said he was "happy to look at how we do it in a gradual way, in order to make sure that it's not just an ideological drive".He separately suggested that he may spend extra funds that come to the Welsh government, as a consequence of more funding for social care in England, on social care in Wales.Labour's Burnham has promised to end triple lock for pensions from 2030 to fund a new national care service.Social care is the responsibility of the Welsh government, and how it spends its money is up to its ministers. Both Plaid and Burnham would face elections before the policy came in.Ap Iorwerth said: "When Boris Johnson was describing his plans that would have led to a consequential [from social care], we in Plaid Cymru were able to put a plan in place at that time that would allow us to spend the consequential on social care in Wales."I would be taking the same approach again."Ap Iorwerth said it was a "good direction of travel" from the prime minister, but he added: "We don't know what the consequentials will be."Ap Iorwerth is expected to meet the prime minister, along with the first ministers of Scotland and Northern Ireland, at the end of the month.Burnham had previously said he would be "open" to the idea of giving the Welsh government control over policing.He has also said: "I have to respect the governments in the nations of the UK, and I will, and give a fair hearing to anything that is put to me."A UK government spokesperson said: "This government is committed to building a stronger and fairer Wales in a stronger and fairer United Kingdom. "That's why our focus is now on working with the Welsh government to empower local leaders and communities to deliver good growth and jobs in every postcode."

schema.headline: First minister demands 'new deal' for Wales, before Plaid Cymru conference

title: Zack Polanski to call for three-year cap on private rent rises
description: Zack Polanski is set to call for a three-year "emergency brake" on private rent increases when he opens the Green Party's conference later.In his spee
body: Zack Polanski is set to call for a three-year "emergency brake" on private rent increases when he opens the Green Party's conference later.In his speech to party activists on Friday afternoon, the Green leader will seek to frame housing as a key issue of generational fairness.He will urge the government to prevent private rents rising above whichever is lowest out of the consumer price index measure of inflation, wage growth or 2%, for three years.According to the party, he will also argue pressure from the Greens has forced Labour into a change of political direction on some issues.The Green Party of England and Wales is billing the gathering in Brighton as its biggest ever, after announcing earlier this year that its membership had tripled since Polanski's election as leader just over a year ago.In his speech, Polanski is expected to say generations are having to live with their parents because of rent prices, from 19-year-olds commuting to university, 25-year-olds unable to find a job, to 35-year-olds moving back home with their partners. "For too long, landlords have been able to hike prices way beyond wages, leaving renters forced to meet the cost to keep a roof over their heads, cutting back and back and back on everything else," he is expected to say. A slowdown on private rent increases "would give renters vital breathing space" and give time for ministers to create a national Fair Rents Guarantee that keeps rents affordable for the future, he is expected to say.Earlier this year, the government brought in the Renters' Rights Act under which landlords can only increase rent once a year to the property's open market rate.Average UK monthly private rents increased by 3.5%, to £1,377, in the 12 months to January 2026, according to the Office for National Statistics.The Act also means tenancies are rolling rather than fixed term, and makes it harder for landlords to evict tenants. But Polanski is expected to argue it does not go far enough in ending "fear and uncertainty" for the millions of private renters in the UK.The Institute for Fiscal Studies has previously warned, external that rent controls - an issue the Greens have long campaigned for - would result in "unintended consequences" including demand exceeding supply in the rental market.However, the party's co-deputy leader Rachel Millward told BBC Breakfast most landlords were "super-earners", who were making more money than other sectors and "would be able to absorb a slight reduction in rent".The Green conference follows the party gaining hundreds of councillors earlier this year at England's local elections and its fifth MP, Hannah Spencer, in the Gorton and Denton by-election.But there are signs its rise in national polls may have stalled in recent months, while the party also faces questions over how to react to Labour's change of leadership under Andy Burnham.Since Burnham became prime minister, Labour has shifted its stance in a number of areas where it had been in danger of being outflanked politically by the Greens.In an interview ahead of the conference, Millward said Labour was now "rhetorically, on a much more similar ground" to her party.This includes Burnham's move towards electoral reform, where the Greens have long demanded a shake-up of the Westminster voting system, and opening the door to a much closer future relationship with the European Union.Labour has also announced sanctions on Israeli West Bank settlements deemed illegal under international law, and the reopening of a scheme to resettle refugees. Speaking ahead of the conference, Polanski claimed those two policies were a result of the electoral pressure his party has applied to Labour.The timing of the conference could, however, prove awkward for Polanski, who is standing for the Greens in next week's Holborn and St Pancras by-election triggered by Sir Keir Starmer's decision to leave Parliament.Polanski said last week he was intending to come "straight back" to the central London seat after his leader's speech.He has even urged the party's activists to leave the conference over the weekend to help him campaign.Victory in the contest would give the Greens their first seat in the capital, but would require them to overturn a huge Labour majority from the last election in 2024. A full list of candidates can be found here.Correction - an earlier version of this story incorrectly said Green Party MP Hannah Spencer won a by-election in Makerfield. She actually won the by-election in Gorton and Denton.

schema.headline: Zack Polanski to call for three-year cap on private rent rises

title: Sir Alex Ferguson on brain haemorrhage and games that shaped his life
description: Ferguson on being 'terrified' by brain haemorrhage and 'fantastic' return to Man UtdFigure caption, Ferguson on Man Utd return, St Johnstone and Class
body: Ferguson on being 'terrified' by brain haemorrhage and 'fantastic' return to Man UtdFigure caption, Ferguson on Man Utd return, St Johnstone and Class of 92ByNeil JohnstonBBC Sport journalist"I was terrified," says Sir Alex Ferguson, one of the fiercest, most explosive and most decorated managers in football history.The legendary former Manchester United boss is recalling the day he returned to Old Trafford for the first time after suffering a brain haemorrhage in May 2018.Four months after emergency surgery, Ferguson - famous for his 'hairdryer treatment' when United dominated English football - was back to watch his beloved club take on Wolves in the Premier League.The man responsible for making the dreams of United fans around the world come true for once was unsure of the reception he would receive from supporters. "I wish I could say I was comfortable. I wasn't," Ferguson tells BBC Breakfast.He need not have worried.Ferguson and his wife Cathy received a standing ovation when they took their seats in the directors' box before kick-off."My wife was with me, and she was nearly crying," he said. "When we sat down, she said:  'That's fantastic.'"Ferguson had been retired five years - after winning 38 trophies during 26 years in charge of United - at the time of his brain haemorrhage, aged 76.Now three months short of 85, he says: "I'm feeling quite good despite small injuries."The Scot has a new book coming out - 'Games of My Life'. It tells the stories of 21 defining matches in his playing and managerial career, revealing fresh insights into his journey from working-class Glasgow to dominating the English game - and Europe - as United boss.Ferguson is thankful he is able to talk about the games that helped shape him. "I had lost my voice; I couldn't speak," he says about the days immediately after brain surgery. "That was a frightening moment."I remember my grandsons coming to see me and I had lost my voice."Then they brought in a therapist and she started doing things like asking me to write down the names of birds, names of animals, names of rivers."That way my voice came back."'I almost quit football for Canada'Ferguson won the lot during his time in charge of United between 1986 and 2013, including 13 Premier League titles.He transformed them into a winning machine, and the history and tradition of United ran red through his veins.As well as delivering two Champions League titles, Ferguson masterminded five FA Cup triumphs, won the League Cup four times and added the Club World Cup, European Super Cup, European Cup Winners' Cup and the Intercontinental Cup to the Old Trafford trophy cabinet.In his book, Ferguson has picked standout games in his career, from winning his first cup final playing for Govan High School in Glasgow in 1955 at the age of 13 through to his retirement as a manager in 2013."That was my starting point," he says, holding the medal he received after that cup win 71 years ago."I played for Glasgow Schools, Scotland Schools and the Scotland youth team. The starting point of my career was there and I can look back with great satisfaction."Ferguson describes growing up in Govan as "the making of me". He says he developed his inner confidence from his mother Elizabeth and a drive to succeed from his father Alexander, who worked in the Govan shipyards on the River Clyde."He was so proud of me and my brother," says Ferguson."He was a hard taskmaster because whenever I scored a hat-trick or a goal, my mother would say 'that's great, son'." His father, meanwhile, offered tough constructive criticism however many goals Ferguson had scored.After making his debut as a 16-year-old striker for Queen's Park, Ferguson ended up at St Johnstone, where he endured a frustrating spell and nearly quit football for a new life in Canada."I wasn't enjoying it. I wasn't playing first-team football; I was in the reserves all the time," he says."I filled out all the forms and phoned my aunt in Canada, because you needed a sponsor then, and never told my mother and father."The next day St Johnstone, decimated by a flu bug in the team, arrived at Ibrox to take on Rangers. A 21-year-old Ferguson was promoted to the starting XI and scored a hat-trick.  That life-changing performance in 1963 revived his playing career and set him on the path to becoming one of football's greatest managers."I would say this to young people - don't miss the biggest opportunity in your life. It's recognising it."Image caption, Ferguson took charge of 1,500 Manchester United games between 1986 and 2013'Don't sell Ince to Inter - or you'll regret it'Ferguson is sat in front of a table for the interview, which was conducted before the Premier League announced on Tuesday that Manchester City had been found guilty of all charges relating to breaches of financial regulations between 2009-10 and 2017-18.On the table are several items from his career, including the Scotland cap he was finally presented with in 2021 - 54 years after appearing for his country.Ferguson received the cap at Hampden Park on the night Scott McTominay - then a United player - scored a dramatic stoppage-time winner in a 3-2 win over Israel in a World Cup qualifier."I remember signing McTominay at seven years of age," Ferguson says.Also on the table are old letters addressed to Ferguson from disgruntled United fans amid speculation he was about to sell midfielder Paul Ince to Inter Milan in the summer of 1995.One reads: 'Don't sell Incey to Inter - or you'll regret it'. Another reads: 'Every Red is disgusted with you'."Paul was a tremendous footballer, there's no doubt about that," says Ferguson."He had incredible ability, but I just had that feeling that he just got carried away a bit at the time."He then got this offer from Inter Milan. I'm trying to weigh up one thing against the other. I'm looking at Paul Scholes and I said 'should we?'"Milan's offer went from £7m to £7.5m and I said 'do it'."That's what your job is as a manager. You have to make hard decisions, and some decisions don't suit everyone."There is also a notebook on the table with a list of words scribbled down by Ferguson when he used to address his players.The names of Bernard "Monty" Montgomery, the World War Two general who outwitted his arch rival, and former prime minister Winston Churchill are on the list. So too is Ince."I didn't notice that before. I couldn't escape him," laughs Ferguson, who once called Ince a "big-time Charlie"., external"I regret saying that. That was a mistake," Ferguson would later say.The pair have since reconciled. "He's a good friend of mine," says Ferguson. "He used to come over and play snooker with me. He texted me not so long ago."'Beckham thought I was trying to get rid'"You can't win anything with kids," former Liverpool and Scotland defender Alan Hansen said after a youthful United side lost 3-1 at Aston Villa in August 1995.Ince, 27, and forward Mark Hughes, 31, had been moved on in the summer to Inter and Chelsea respectively.Meanwhile, Ryan Giggs, 21, Gary Neville, 20, Scholes, 20, and David Beckham, 20, were beginning to make a name for themselves.By the end of the season, Ferguson's side had won the Premier League and FA Cup double."We'd worked really hard getting youth into the club again and this bunch of young lads became the spirit of Manchester United," says Ferguson. "They added something. Apart from the great abilities they had, they had desire. I put Beckham out on loan at Preston [in March 1995] and he thought I was trying to get rid of him, which was not true."David was the last to really develop because of his physique. Although he grew to 6ft, he was small and thin as a young kid."Did Ferguson ever fear that throwing his young players in at the deep end could backfire?"I did exactly the same when I was in charge at St Mirren and Aberdeen," he says."I had belief in young people because if you give them an opportunity there are two things that happen - they become real stars and they can remain loyal to you as a manager."Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Manchester United's famous 'Class of 92', including Ryan Giggs (second left), David Beckham (fourth left), Gary Neville (fourth right) and Paul Scholes (second right)Follow Manchester United on BBC SoundsPre-match, post-match and topical United contentSubscribe and listen for everything you love about the Red Devils

schema.headline: Sir Alex Ferguson on brain haemorrhage and games that shaped his life

title: Manchester City charges: What does guilty verdict mean for players?
description: So much has been said about Manchester City since it was revealed they had been found guilty of the majority of the 115 Premier League charges levelle
body: So much has been said about Manchester City since it was revealed they had been found guilty of the majority of the 115 Premier League charges levelled at them.On Tuesday, it was confirmed that an independent commission found City guilty of all charges relating to breaches of the league's financial regulations between the 2009-10 and 2017-18 seasons. The club has repeatedly denied guilt. Their potential punishment has been debated, the future of the owners questioned and the feelings of the rest of the league - and wider football world - have been aired.But so far there has been little focus on what it means for one crucial group.Their current squad.Without definitive clarity on what sanctions the Premier League will impose, pending City's inevitable appeal, which must be lodged by Friday, there is uncertainty over their ability to retain players, renew contracts, and make transfers - and whether any of the team have release clauses.Put simply, will players want to join? Will current players want to stay?BBC Sport has spoken to a number of sources in an attempt to understand how the recent judgement will impact City's dealings in the transfer market and how existing players may approach their futures with the prospect of losing Premier League status hanging over the club.The general train of thought is that any drop down the leagues for City will result in a mass exodus.That players will, at the very least, consider their futures at Etihad Stadium in the event of demotion would be understandable.The squad is brimming with international talent, many of whose profiles and personal sponsorship agreements benefit from plying their trade in the Premier League.The reaction from current members of the City squad varies depending on who you speak to.From the conversations BBC Sport have had with sources close to the first team, there is certainly a significant level of concern as to how they will be affected.Given the scathing tone of the Premier League's statement on Tuesday, there is major scepticism from people close to the players that the forthcoming appeals will earn the club any reprieve.But there are others who absolutely believe in City executives Khaldoon Al Mubarak and Ferran Soriano's vows to prove the club's innocence.For those players who decide they don't want to drop down the divisions, should it come to that, the process of leaving is unlikely to be straightforward.Firstly there is the contract and the player registrations. City, regardless of each individual's view on whether they want to depart, have the right to demand transfer fees.Given how much those players are worth in terms of wages and their general value in the market you'd imagine City are unlikely to accept being undercut.That, as BBC Sport understands, the majority of players do not have relegation clauses in their contracts also plays into the club's hands.But it is also understood that as a general rule the players' contracts are fully guaranteed, meaning they would not be required to take percentage pay cuts if they lose their top-flight status.With one of the highest wage bills in the world, maintaining that level of salary expenditure, even for a club as financially capable as City, will become harder without Premier League-level income.Parachute money could ease those concerns, although there are no guarantees that the club would be entitled to those payments if they are demoted.With that in mind, City deciding to keep the squad completely intact should they move down the leagues appears unlikely.How amenable City are to selling players will be dependent on how bullish they are about it all.Are they a distressed seller? Probably not. They still hold strong control of the situation regardless of how their players may feel.It is unlikely the club will just simply roll over and let disillusioned players depart without suitable offers because, ultimately, they can ride the storm financially.Players will have massive decisions to make too, not just in respect of leaving.City are big payers, and other clubs may not be willing to meet similar wage demands."Some players want medals, all players want money," one agent said to BBC Sport.In terms of potential contract renewals, the current uncertainty over what sanctions will be meted out provides a major element of risk.Amending a contract retrospectively, say for example to include a relegation clause, generally cannot happen.Any deals that include exit strategies for players if the club fall out of the Premier League would have to be negotiated as new contracts.Players will likely want to wait for clarity on the sanctions before entering into contract discussions, adding a layer of difficulty for the club.One way round persuading a player to renew would be to offer a significant financial incentive to re-sign to negate the risk of relegation.But a number of agents who spoke to BBC Sport believe players will be advised to wait for clarity on the punishments before even considering opening talks.Thankfully for City, only Mateo Kovacic, Matheus Nunes, Marcus Bettinelli and Geronimo Rulli have contracts expiring in the next two summers, so that issue isn't as urgent as it could have been.City's potential challenges with player contracts comes with Fifa preparing to introduce new rules that state every deal signed on 1 January, 2027 or after must include a release clause.The looming punishment certainly complicates City's plans in the transfer market."This isn't the players' failing, it's on the club. Potential new signings aren't even in the building and joining City without knowing what the punishment would be represents an undeniable risk, so any new contracts would have to have indemnities," said one leading agent.It was acknowledged that writing eventualities into new registrations is very difficult, though City players do have release clauses in their deals should the club enter into administration.Until a post-appeal verdict over sanctions is made, making new signings will certainly become more complicated, though it is still likely they will be able to attract big players as they still have the financial muscle to do so.For example, one potential method of persuading a player to join would be to offer them a contract on big money with no pay decreases if the club are relegated, and then include a fixed fee release clause if City don't return to the top flight within a set period.If sanctions ensure relegation and include further points deductions that stretch over multiple seasons, attracting top players will of course be harder.City could make a wage package hard to resist for elite players, but it seems inconceivable that a footballer of that ilk would join with demotion a possibility as there are likely to be other top options elsewhere.The same logic can be applied to the retention of their current squad.There is almost certainly going to be interest in their top players from other elite clubs across Europe. It will be very difficult for City to keep that level of player in the coming months and years while the saga plays out.So with all that said, particularly if relegation is confirmed, City will have to rebuild their squad to some extent, though the prospect of a transfer embargo as one of the sanctions would prevent them from making any signings at all.Such a rebuild may include the promotion of some of the club's best academy players, who stand to benefit if the first-team squad disbands.When Chelsea were placed under a transfer embargo in 2019, the likes of Mason Mount, Tammy Abraham, Fikayo Tomori, Billy Gilmour and Callum Hudson-Odoi all emerged as senior players.And while City may look to rebuild with a profile of player they believe will be adept at being successful in the EFL, you will likely see a number of their younger players fast-tracked.With that said, a number of clubs are already working on seeing if they can capitalise on the current uncertainty by luring City's best academy talent.

schema.headline: Manchester City charges: What does guilty verdict mean for players?

title: From Edinburgh to Easter Island: How my stolen Ian Wright Celtic top went round the world
description: But such was Kevin's affection that long after it was over, the green-and-white hooped jersey remained his go-to match day uniform.It was particularly
body: But such was Kevin's affection that long after it was over, the green-and-white hooped jersey remained his go-to match day uniform.It was particularly distinctive as it featured his hero's name, but not the number 17.Kevin explained: "The reason it doesn't have a number on the back was because he hadn't actually signed yet and so we didn't know his number when I got it."So when the strip went missing he was gutted. Having recently moved to Edinburgh, he assumed that someone had helped themselves during a fairly raucous flat-warming party.While he had suspicions, he could never identify the culprit. Over time, however, his anger faded and he'd largely forgotten about it when, years later, an email arrived in his inbox from an account he didn't recognise.It began: "Hi Kevin, remember me? Yes that's right, it's your Ian Wright Celtic strip."The message continued: "I hope you aren't mad with me but I decided to embark on a journey of discovery."When Kevin opened the attached photograph it featured a woman he didn't know on the London Eye holding up what appeared to be his Celtic top to the camera."I was just mega confused," he says."Running through my mind was, who has done this? "I mean bravo, it's a really good prank."But little did I know there were a lot more emails to follow."A few weeks later another message arrived. Once again it contained a photo of a complete stranger wearing Kev's prized possession – this time in Barcelona.After that the emails kept on coming."The next one was Turkey, then Italy and then it went all the way to South America," Kevin recalls."Christ the Redeemer was one of my favourite ones. "It made it all the way [to Brazil] and then down to Venezuela and Puerto Rico and then back up to the USA."Friends since their schooldays, Kris Robertson vividly remembers Kevin's fondness for his Ian Wright Celtic strip."He used to wear it all the time. I just remember he was very proud of it. It was his prize possession."That affection made it the ideal source of payback after Kevin hijacked Kris's emails with the aim of embarrassing him at work."It was revenge," says the 48-year-old, smiling.Revenge that took unlikely inspiration from French cinema. Part of the plot in the 2001 movie Amelie involves the main character stealing her dad's garden gnome and sending it around the world."It was postcards with pictures of all these exotic locations and I thought that's perfect, I've got to do that with his strip."As the strip racked up the air miles Kris kept drip-feeding the emails to his unsuspecting friend"At one point I did get an email back [from Kevin] saying I think I've worked out who it is."I knew he hadn't and of course I never heard from him again. He was obviously trying to flush me out."A great prank, however, requires a big reveal. Which, after years of deception, was something Kris agonised over."When he announced he was getting married, I thought this is the perfect opportunity."When the moment arrived Kris says the confused look on Kevin's face was worth it: "It was really good. I knew he'd appreciate the gag and finally finding out but it was actually a bit of a relief as well. I couldn't keep this going forever."Kris's mum and dad were among those who helped him build up a bank of photos from around the UK and Europe. Then in 2008 he took the strip with him to South America where the prank took on a life of its own."I met people in Peru and I gave them the strip because they were going off travelling around the world."They took it away with them and went to Easter Island with the big stone heads.They went to Christ the Redeemer in Rio. They got some brilliant photos."There is, however, a twist – a confession Kris hasn't been brave enough to make until now.Sometime around 2013 the steady stream of photos he'd been receiving from around the world suddenly stopped.When he contacted the last person he knew had the strip, they sheepishly confessed to losing it."I suppose that's the risk of sending it off around the world with complete strangers."Kris was determined the prank he'd invested so much time and energy into wouldn't just fizzle out.So he spent hours scouring the internet for a replacement strip and identical lettering which, in the end, he had to iron on by hand."I should apologise yes it was very careless of me to lose [but] a lot of love went back into the replacement."Which raises the intriguing prospect that more than a quarter of a century on, the original "Wrighty" is out there somewhere, searching for a way home.This epic tale of love, loss, revenge and reconciliation might still have room for another chapter.

schema.headline: From Edinburgh to Easter Island: How my stolen Ian Wright Celtic top went round the world

title: Chris Mason: Why Andy Burnham's about-turn on Manchester City matters
description: The rows circulating around Manchester City are huge, and they are only going to get bigger.The Premier League has concluded that City "systematically
body: The rows circulating around Manchester City are huge, and they are only going to get bigger.The Premier League has concluded that City "systematically broke Premier League Rules for nearly a decade".This, clearly, matters for the club, but that is just the start of it. It matters for Manchester, it matters for the Premier League and so, crucially, it matters for the UK's image around the world – because England's top flight is a colossal global brand. In other words, this matters whether you like football or not.Added to all of this, Andy Burnham pitches himself as Mr Manchester and is a big football fan. The man who was the mayor of Greater Manchester a matter of months ago is now the prime minister, and so finds himself caught up in it all at a local level, a national level and a diplomatic level. Diplomatic, because rows will rage over the extent to which City's ownership is separate from the Abu Dhabi state. And the state is a big UK ally.All of this is why I thought it was in the public interest to put a series of questions to Burnham about it when I spoke to him on Wednesday as the Labour Party conference concluded in Liverpool.His comments, in his interview with me, followed by no fewer than two attempts to backtrack 24 hours later, amount to perhaps his biggest self inflicted tangle since he arrived in Downing Street in July.He will have expected to be asked about Manchester City, but he didn't expect sustained scrutiny about it.One particular exchange prompted a lot of interest. I asked if he was worried that Manchester City's owners from the United Arab Emirates might sell up.It is worth quoting his answer in full."Well, I would be really concerned to lose them. They've been such a huge partner in the building of modern Manchester. Obviously, the building of Manchester City into the global force that it is. "I can't intervene more in the process. It would be wrong for me to do that. It would be wrong, I think, to jump to a conclusion before having really studied all of the detail, but obviously it's ongoing, and because it's still contested by Manchester City, then I think it's right that I don't say much more."His answer is revealing on several levels, and was leapt on by many in football and then by the Conservatives, who labelled them "completely out of touch" and "extraordinary".Firstly, his fear – being "really concerned" – that the vast money from Abu Dhabi, that has transformed not just the club but parts of the city, could go.Secondly, that "I can't intervene more" in the process that is ongoing. What does "more" mean?To be fair, as you can see in the full quote above and he said repeatedly elsewhere in the interview, he was trying to be circumspect about it all."I am not getting directly involved in the process," he told me, later adding "I have to keep my distance from it."But, the cumulative impression many were left with was that he was sympathetic to Manchester City's situation, not least because he repeatedly compared it to a vastly smaller row involving his own club Everton's finances a few years ago."I remember people proclaiming Everton guilty at the time, and you know, with hindsight, I think more people would say that wasn't fair the way that was handled. So it would be wrong of me to leap to one side given the experience that I'd had before becoming prime minister."Everton were docked Premier League points over it.Despite the gravity and breadth of what Manchester City now confront, Andy Burnham offered no explicit criticism of them.The back pages and the sports channels as well as news sites and social media were quickly ablaze with the remarks.And by teatime on Thursday, No10 were back-pedalling.A written statement was sent out, which again is worth quoting in full:"As the prime minister made clear, the initial judgement is serious and there can't be any suggestion that anyone is above the rules. He also stressed that it is an ongoing independent process. It is essential that it is allowed to run its course and the outcome respected."If wrongdoing is established, those responsible should face the appropriate consequences."Some 59 words that could be replaced by a picture of a reversing light – the tone and language completely different from Burnham's to me on camera.But even that statement didn't last long. Immediately, the first word of the second paragraph of it was jumped on. "If."Remember, the Premier League says Manchester City arranged "sham contracts" with a number of commercial partners as part of a scheme to disguise secret funding of almost a billion pounds. The club deny wrongdoing and are considering an appeal, but the Premier League's conclusion is clear.But Downing Street said "if." Fast forward a little over an hour, and the statement was re-issued. "If" became "wherever."In real time, No10's jitters and discomfort about this was there for all to see.The prime minister seen as Mr Manchester, who loves his football and revels in a man of the people image, caught up in one of the biggest domestic stories of the year and one that is only just beginning.It won't be the last time he faces questions about Manchester City.

schema.headline: Chris Mason: Why Andy Burnham's about-turn on Manchester City matters
